content: The approach and potential refinements of the described methods are still under validation and may require further adjustments. If the survey is based on sampling designs other than Respondent-Driven Sampling (RDS), the described method may not be suitable. Recently, Dombrowski et al. utilized a one-sample capture-recapture (CRC) method entirely within a biobehavioral survey (BBS). This innovative approach employed a network-based variant of CRC, ensuring participant anonymity. The method involved sampling from each participant’s network connections and matching these connections against other participants in the sample and their respective contact lists. The initial capture was conducted using RDS via an online platform (e.g., Craigslist), while the second capture was based on respondents’ personal network connections. Recapture sampling relied on demographic and anonymized telephone number matching procedures, referred to as telefunken. This technique allowed for population size estimation without the need for physically recruiting a second sample. All population size estimation methods have inherent limitations. Estimates are often uncertain, and different methods may yield varying results. Factors contributing to uncertainty include variability in the quality of service data (multiplier method), challenges in meeting assumptions (CRC), and transmission errors (Network Scale-Up Method, NSUM). Using multiple methods for population size estimation is recommended, as it provides checks, balances, and cross-validation. When different methods produce estimates within the same range, confidence in the results increases compared to relying on a single method. The choice of method and the number of methods used often depend on available resources. Investigators planning size estimation activities should consider integrating multiple methods when designing BBS or other surveys. Formative assessments, including social and geographic mapping and ethnographic observations, should be conducted before implementing a BBS. These assessments can help estimate the accessible population size at specific sites. If a household survey is planned, investigators should explore the feasibility of using NSUM to estimate the size of multiple key populations. Proper planning and preparation are critical before integrating any specific method into a BBS. When planning a BBS, it is essential to assess available resources and capacities to determine which methods can be integrated. For the service multiplier method, it is crucial to evaluate the type, quality, and accessibility of service data, as well as any legal or other constraints. Formative assessments involving key population members can clarify the social and geographic distribution of the target population and inform the selection of appropriate methods. Local estimates derived from BBS cannot be extrapolated to national estimates without additional methods such as data triangulation or NSUM. The social visibility and mobility of the target population are critical considerations. If the population is visible and accessible in specific locations, census or enumeration methods may be appropriate. However, high mobility can complicate census and enumeration efforts and may violate CRC assumptions. For national-level estimates, NSUM is often more suitable, especially when other methods like CRC or multiplier methods are challenging to implement. Financial and technical resources also play a significant role in method selection. Census and enumeration are resource-intensive, depending on the size of the area and the number of venues. In contrast, Bayesian statistics applied to existing RDS data require minimal additional time but demand technical expertise. CRC may require more resources and technical capacity compared to census and enumeration. Service provision data can facilitate the use of the multiplier method when reliable service data are available, and service providers can accurately count target population members. However, venue-based methods may lead to underestimates if not all members of the target population are accessible at venues. Qualitative studies complement BBS by providing insights into the behaviors and meanings attached to them. Formative assessments conducted before a BBS help plan the survey, while supplemental qualitative studies during or after a BBS address additional questions. Together, quantitative and qualitative methods offer a comprehensive understanding of knowledge, behaviors, and practices, informing the design of effective interventions.
